The three-rate decomposition BA = c(h + (1-h)b) provides a structural mathematical unification of batting performance into three distinct components: contact rate (c), home-run rate (h), and batting average on balls in play (b). This formulation reveals that batting average is a composite of skill (contact and power) and luck (BABIP). The identity holds exactly across all players and seasons, implying that any deviation from this structure indicates either measurement error or non-standard behavior. The negative correlation between contact and power (c and h) implies that players who avoid strikes tend to hit fewer home runs, which historically reduced the variance in batting averages and made .400 hitters rare. The stability of c and h (correlations 0.86 and 0.74) versus b (0.41) suggests that contact and power are more reliable indicators of true ability than BABIP. This allows for robust empirical Bayes inference in GSI, where individual batting averages are shrunk toward population means based on these stable traits. In GSE, the decomposition enables modeling of at-bat progression as a Markov chain with state transitions defined by outcome categories: strikeout, home run, or ball in play, each governed by different skill sets.
